## Set Countability

Countability is the first measure of the "size" of a set, and underlies many
arguments in measure theory, for example that the countable/co-countable
collection is a $\sigma$-algebra (see [[set-theory-fundamentals]]).

## Countable and Uncountable Sets

:::{.definition data-title="Countable Set"}

A set $A$ is **countably infinite** if there is a bijection $A\to\mathbb{N}$. It
is **countable** (or **at most countable**) if it is finite or countably
infinite, equivalently if there is an injection $A\to\mathbb{N}$. A set that is
not countable is **uncountable**.

:::

> *Note:* Some authors use "countable" to mean countably infinite. Here
countable includes finite sets.

## Subsets and Images

:::{.theorem data-title="Subsets of Countable Sets"}

Every subset of a countable set is countable.

:::

:::{.proof}
Let $B\subseteq A$ with an injection $f:A\to\mathbb{N}$. Then $f|_B$ is an
injection $B\to\mathbb{N}$, so $B$ is countable.
:::

## Products and Unions

:::{.theorem data-title="Countable Products"}

$\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ is countable. Hence if $A,B$ are countable then so
is $A\times B$.

:::

:::{.proof}
The map $(n,m)\mapsto 2^n3^m$ is an injection $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ by
uniqueness of prime factorisation. For general countable $A,B$ compose with
injections $A\to\mathbb{N}$, $B\to\mathbb{N}$.
:::

:::{.theorem data-title="Countable Union of Countable Sets"}

If $A_n$ is countable for each $n\in\mathbb{N}$ then $\bigcup_{n}A_n$ is countable.

:::

:::{.proof}
For each $n$ choose an injection $f_n:A_n\to\mathbb{N}$. For $x\in\bigcup_nA_n$ let
$n(x)=\min\{n: x\in A_n\}$ and define
$$
F(x)=(n(x),\,f_{n(x)}(x))\in\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}.
$$
Then $F$ is injective, since $F(x)=F(y)$ gives $n(x)=n(y)=n$ and
$f_n(x)=f_n(y)$, so $x=y$. Composing with an injection
$\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ shows the union is countable.
:::

> *Note:* Choosing the injections $f_n$ simultaneously for all $n$ uses the
(countable) Axiom of Choice, see [[vitalli-non-measurability-theorem|Axiom of Choice]].

A finite union or finite product of countable sets is a special case.

## Examples

:::{.example data-title="$\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{Q}$ are Countable"}

$\mathbb{Z}=\mathbb{N}\cup(-\mathbb{N})\cup\{0\}$ is a countable union of countable
sets. Each $\mathbb{Q}_n=\{p/n: p\in\mathbb{Z}\}$ is countable (a bijective image of
$\mathbb{Z}$), so $\mathbb{Q}=\bigcup_{n\geq1}\mathbb{Q}_n$ is countable. In particular
$\mathbb{Q}\cap[0,1]$ is a countable dense subset of $[0,1]$.

:::

## Uncountable Sets

:::{.theorem data-title="$\mathbb{R}$ is Uncountable"}

The interval $(0,1)$, and hence $\mathbb{R}$, is uncountable.

:::

:::{.proof}
(Cantor's diagonal argument.) Suppose $(0,1)=\{x_1,x_2,\dots\}$ and write
$x_n=0.d_{n1}d_{n2}d_{n3}\dots$ in decimal, choosing the expansion not ending
in all $9$s. Define $y=0.e_1e_2\dots$ with $e_n=5$ if $d_{nn}\neq5$ and $e_n=4$
if $d_{nn}=5$. Then $y\in(0,1)$, has no digit $0$ or $9$, so its expansion is
unique, and $y$ differs from each $x_n$ in the $n$-th digit. So $y\neq x_n$ for
all $n$, a contradiction. Since $(0,1)\subseteq\mathbb{R}$, $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable.
:::

More generally, **Cantor's theorem** states that there is no surjection
$X\to2^X$ for any set $X$, so $2^X$ is strictly larger than $X$.
